title: Right livelihood
hook: the Buddha names trades to avoid, such as dealing in weapons and poisons (Anguttara Nikaya 5.177)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ihsan: work done with excellence, as though seen. Your line was excellence. Which task got your full care? Yesterday asked how the work is done. Today asks what the work does. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

Weapons. Living beings. Meat. Intoxicants. Poison. That's the whole list, and it's short. In a discourse kept in the Anguttara Nikaya, one of the collections of the Buddha's teachings, he names five kinds of trade that a lay follower should not take up. He doesn't name priests or kings or bankers. He names what changes hands. A sword. A living being sold. A jar of something that clouds the mind. A vial of something that kills. It's a list about what your work puts into the world. Today's word is the step of the Buddhist path it belongs to.
screen: `FIVE TRADES, ONE SHORT LIST.` → `WHAT CHANGES HANDS.` → `WHAT YOUR WORK PUTS OUT.`

segments.voice: First, where it sits. In the teaching Buddhists call the turning of the wheel of the Dhamma, the Buddha lays out the noble eightfold path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Right livelihood comes just after speech and action. So a job is not set apart from the spiritual life. How you earn is part of the path, the same as how you speak. Second, the list itself. In the Anguttara, the five trades are dealing in weapons, in living beings, in meat, in intoxicants, and in poison. Notice the thread running through them. Each one, in its own way, puts harm into the hands of someone else. Third, who it's for. The Buddha speaks these words to his monks, but the rule isn't about monks. It's about lay followers, people with households and bills. It doesn't tell them to stop working. It tells them which work to leave alone. Buddhist teachers differ on how far to take it today. Some read the list closely and keep to it. Others treat it as a direction more than a fence, and ask a wider question of any job: who does this hurt, and could it hurt less? Fourth, why this is harder than it sounds. A list like this can seem far from an office or a kitchen. But the question underneath the list goes everywhere. A sales target that pushes someone into a loan they can't carry. Food that's cheap because someone, somewhere, is paid too little. The list is short. The question it leaves behind is not.
screen: `A STEP ON THE EIGHTFOLD PATH.` · `WEAPONS, BEINGS, MEAT, DRINK, POISON.` · `A RULE FOR PEOPLE WITH JOBS.` · `WHO DOES THIS HURT?` · then, large: `RIGHT LIVELIHOOD.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath slow. Let one piece of your work come to mind, just one. A product you sell, a message you send, a meal you cook, a decision you sign off on. Hold it the way you'd hold a cup, turning it slowly in your hands. Ask the discourse's question of it: does anything harmful change hands here? Often the answer may be no. If something does come up, don't argue with it. Let it sit beside the breath. Then ask a smaller question: what one change would make it a little less harmful? If you pray, you can bring this question in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Right livelihood. A step on the Buddha's eightfold path: earning a living in a way that does not deal in harm. Today's word.
Your line: right livelihood. Today, ask once of your work: does this harm anyone, and could it harm less? Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhists list right livelihood as one step of the noble eightfold path, and Buddhist teachers often raise it when lay followers ask how to choose or carry out their work.

original.note: Pali, from the Buddhist suttas: right livelihood, the fifth step of the eightfold path.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice way of saying a good job.
what it means: a step on the Buddha's eightfold path, earning a living without dealing in harm.
what a scholar hears: the Anguttara's five trades, weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants and poison, spoken to monks but given as a rule for lay followers with households.

notes: The five trades of AN 5.177 are paraphrased (weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants, poison); 'living beings' is often explained as human trafficking/slaves. Confirm wording.
The eightfold path is listed in order from SN 56.11; the original-game note calls right livelihood 'the fifth step' per that order. Confirm.
Pali 'samma ajiva' given in Devanagari as सम्मा आजीव; a Buddhist Keeper should confirm the spelling and the pronunciation guide.
'Buddhist teachers differ on how far to take it today' is an attribution without names or counts; confirm phrasing.
SN 56.11 is described only as what Buddhists call the turning of the wheel of the Dhamma; no 'first sermon' claim is made.

Editor: fixed the claim that right livelihood sits next to speech (it follows speech and action) in the teach and match game, changed 'a person sold' to 'a living being sold' to match the text, and replaced the practice (following your work outward to who it serves repeated day 891) with turning one piece of work over and asking what harm changes hands.

Audit: AN 5.177 is addressed to the monks (bhikkhave) and states what a lay follower (upasaka) should not trade in; the script wrongly said it was addressed to lay followers 'not to monks'. Teach, teach screen head, match pair and trapdoor corrected.
